chunks: Why a gate pulldown resistor. The question: Why would a pulldown resistor be necessary?
A MOSFET's gate (its control pin) is insulated from the rest of the transistor, so it acts like a tiny capacitor that draws almost no steady current.
If nothing drives it, it does not sit at zero: it keeps whatever voltage it last had and drifts with leakage and noise.
A pulldown resistor from gate to ground gives that gate a defined path to 0 volts, so the switch stays off whenever the microcontroller is not driving it.
Imagine a swing door with no latch and no spring. It could sit open, closed or halfway, depending on the draft. A pulldown is a spring that always pulls the door shut.
Pushing the door open on purpose takes only a little extra effort.
The analogy leaves out one limit: a weak spring cannot hold the door against a strong gust, like a fast voltage jump on a bridge.
With the GPIO high-impedance (reset or input), leakage and coupled noise (the arrow) have nowhere to go except R pd .
They create V equals I leakR pd : 100 nanoamps through 100 kilohms is 10 millivolts, nowhere near the threshold.
High-impedance (Hi-Z) pin: a pin that is not driving high or low, as in reset or input mode. Floating: a wire with no steady connection, so leakage and pickup set its voltage.
Threshold voltage ( V th ): the gate voltage where the transistor starts to conduct.
Linear region: the half-on state where the FET drops real voltage while carrying current, so it heats up.
Pulldown resistor: a resistor, here 10 to 100 kilohms, from gate to ground.
A 12 volts supply drives a 24 ohms coil through a FET. If the floating gate leaves the FET half on and 0. 25 amps flows, the coil drops 0. 25 times 24 equals 6 volts.
The FET drops the other 6 volts, so it dissipates 6 times 0. 25 equals 1. 5 watts, a lot for a small package.
With a 100 kilohms pulldown, the gate sits at 0 volts when the pin is Hi-Z, and the FET stays off. When the pin drives 3. 3 volts, the pulldown draws only 3.
3 over 100 k equals 33 microamps. That is the whole idea.

"A MOSFET gate is a capacitor with a huge DC resistance, so if the driving pin is in reset, booting or set as an input, the gate floats and drifts with leakage and noise, and can drift above threshold.
Then the FET half-turns on and either fires the load at power-up or sits in its linear region burning power.
A 10 to 100 kilohms pulldown from gate to source gives the gate a defined path to ground so it defaults off, and costs only microamps when the pin drives it high."
